Even work described as handmade depends on energy moving through supply chains, workshops, and tools. Vey argues that tracing those flows is not an optional supplement to studying craft: it reveals conditions inherent in how the work becomes possible.

Text 2
An energy-based account can be useful without capturing what matters most in a craft workshop. Consider a cabinetmaker teaching apprentices to judge a joint by touch. Lighting the room and drying the timber certainly consume energy, but the most meaningful exchange occurs when an experienced hand guides an uncertain one. Measuring the electricity used would not by itself describe that learning.
questions.question: How would Vey most likely respond to the workshop example in Text 2?

choices.A: By emphasizing that aspects of the example itself demonstrate craft production's dependence on energy flows
choices.B: By agreeing that hand-guided instruction is invariably more valuable than all other parts of production
choices.C: By rejecting Text 2's claim that a craft workshop can be operated without any energy use
choices.D: By questioning whether knowledge of workshop resource use leads apprentices to become engaged in craft

questions.explanation: A is supported by Text 2's acknowledgment of lighting and timber drying, which illustrates Vey's contention even if it does not describe the learning itself. B adds a value ranking Vey never gives. C misrepresents Text 2, which explicitly acknowledges energy use. D changes the issue to apprentices' engagement, an unexamined relationship. Vey can point to inherent energy conditions without claiming that an energy measure exhausts the significance of every human interaction.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Weighted sounding lines, portable tools used to measure water depth, appeared along widely separated coasts long before modern electronic instruments. Fishing communities in Portugal relied on them, as did navigators in Senegal. A 1704 account by court chronicler Nerem Val described their use aboard visiting vessels, even though Val himself worked in an inland administrative center. The tool thus reached observers as well as sailors outside any single maritime community.

Text 2
Names translated as “sounding line” and “bottom finder” can refer to the same basic arrangement: a weighted cord lowered until it reaches the seabed. Different coastal communities used local names and markings, but the instrument's association with navigation and fishing is consistent. Its history belongs to several seafaring regions rather than exclusively to the coast most often linked with it.
questions.question: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Sounding lines became substantially more accurate as they spread from Portugal to Senegal.
choices.B: Portable depth-measuring lines were known and used in more than one coastal region.
choices.C: Nerem Val played a central role in inventing and popularizing sounding lines.
choices.D: Despite their maritime associations, sounding lines have become permanent land-based instruments in some modern cultures.

questions.explanation: B is supported by Text 1's named regional uses and Text 2's account of several seafaring communities. A adds an unreported progression in accuracy. C turns an observer and chronicler into an inventor and promoter. D invents a modern transformation into land-based instruments. Differences in naming do not obscure the shared point that knowledge and use of the tool crossed regional boundaries.

questions.passage:
The following text is from Kosta Velra's 1904 novel The Clockmaker's Notebook. A twelve-year-old apprentice narrates this opening to the second part of his account.

If the first pages seemed tedious, I can only say that you would have understood none of our trouble without knowing what each wheel was meant to do. Lists are poor company in a story, though they may be necessary at its door. What interests me is the moment a mechanism refuses its assigned task; things that work exactly as expected scarcely seem to have happened at all. Accordingly, I shall pass over the weeks when every clock kept time and begin where the quiet stopped.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To apologize for the narrator's preference for one kind of book over another
choices.B: To identify several books that influenced the narrator's taste
choices.C: To relate decisions about the narrator's own account to principles the narrator expresses
choices.D: To recall a decisive episode in the narrator's formal schooling

questions.explanation: C is correct because the narrator explains both including preliminary information and omitting uneventful weeks through stated ideas about what makes a story intelligible and interesting. A reduces the passage to an apology about taste, missing its explanation of actual writing choices. B invents named influences. D mistakes reflection on narrative organization for a remembered school episode. The apprentice's preference matters because it governs how this account is arranged.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Sera Almir's 1878 poem “North in Brass,” translated from Italian by Nadia Coen in 1924. Kerval is a mountain pass mentioned in the poem.

Needle of mine,
Small, steady light,
Wealth without coin,
Keeper of right.
When maps grow pale
And markers fail,
You keep your bearing,
My silence sharing.
From Kerval's broken stair
Through roads that lead nowhere,
Your patient point remains
Above my doubts and pains.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the poem?

choices.A: To express the value the speaker places on a dependable guiding instrument
choices.B: To convey the speaker's confusion after a single extraordinary occurrence
choices.C: To emphasize the uncertainty of the instrument's directional readings
choices.D: To suggest that the speaker wishes to erase memories of a difficult journey

questions.explanation: A fits the descriptions of the needle as wealth, a keeper of direction, and a steady presence when other guides fail. B invents a specific extraordinary event; the poem describes recurring conditions. C reverses the needle's steadiness and persistent bearing. D adds a wish to forget, whereas the speaker values what continues to offer support. The doubts belong to the traveler, not to the instrument's ability to guide.

questions.passage:
The following text is from Elian Sore's 1927 short story “Glass at Closing.” The narrator is walking alone through an old glassworks late in the afternoon.

Nothing in the long hall seemed quite level: the rails curved gently toward the furnaces, and the windows rose by unequal steps beneath the roof. Far beyond the nearest racks, the cold mouths of two furnaces could just be seen, framed by girders whose shadows crossed the floor. A soft band of sunlight lay over the hanging sheets of glass, turning their rough edges briefly gold. From a half-open ventilator came a mild current of air and the faint, irregular tapping of a loose pane.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To celebrate the unpretentious lives of the workers who use the glassworks
choices.B: To argue that difficult movement through a building deepens appreciation of its beauty
choices.C: To convey impressions of a particular industrial setting at a particular time
choices.D: To show how the same hall appears fundamentally different at morning and evening

questions.explanation: C accounts for the spatial features, shadows, sunlight, airflow, and sound observed during one afternoon visit. A invents a depiction of workers' lives; no workers appear. B adds both travel difficulty and a causal claim about appreciation. D requires two observed times, whereas the excerpt describes one. The setting's irregular surfaces contribute to an impression, not to a developed argument or comparison.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Rian Tever's proposed footbridge over the Sarel Canal drew criticism for an element unrelated to its elegant arches: both approaches ended in steep stairways. Local residents petitioned for access that would accommodate wheelchairs and cargo bicycles. Public discussions emphasized that a bridge advertised as connecting neighborhoods would exclude some of their residents in routine use. The controversy ultimately led the municipality to withdraw the proposal.

Text 2
Tever's canal bridge drew on the precisely curved structural designs of twentieth-century engineer Ivara Soran. Its paired arches were intended to produce a balanced outline with few visible supports. Though the project was later discontinued, civic chair Nadia Morven called its geometry “inventive and exceptionally assured” when the design was unveiled in 2018.
questions.question: How would the author of Text 1 most likely respond to Morven's assessment in Text 2?

choices.A: By arguing that the design's departure from earlier engineering styles caused its rejection
choices.B: By explaining that a practical access feature undermined the project despite its admired geometry
choices.C: By asserting that a small revision would certainly have preserved every feature of the original design
choices.D: By describing the steep approaches as simultaneously controversial and geometrically revolutionary

questions.explanation: B follows Text 1's distinction between admired arches and inaccessible approaches. The design could receive aesthetic praise while failing a practical requirement. A conflicts with Text 2's stated continuity with earlier designs. C assumes the feasibility and scope of a revision that neither text establishes. D transfers praise of the geometry to the stairways without support. The author would identify the reason praise did not secure the project's acceptance.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Experienced members of scientific review panels do not need anonymity merely to escape dismissal; their reputations already command attention. A study of 27 panels instead suggests that anonymous first-round notes improve their analytical work. With names removed, senior reviewers can explore uncertain interpretations without having every tentative suggestion treated as an authoritative verdict. The study associates that separation of statement and status with more candid evaluation.

Text 2
Anonymous notes can benefit senior reviewers' deliberations, but that is not their only use. Junior participants lack the established standing that protects senior colleagues from being ignored. Keeping names off initial comments can prevent a useful observation from being discounted simply because its author is new. The same procedure can therefore aid participants at different stages for different reasons.
questions.question: How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the findings discussed in Text 1?

choices.A: By disputing that anonymous notes can improve senior reviewers' analytical work
choices.B: By insisting that reviewers in different scientific disciplines obtain sharply different benefits from anonymity
choices.C: By faulting the study for drawing conclusions from too few review panels
choices.D: By noting that anonymity can usefully serve both junior and senior reviewers

questions.explanation: D is correct because Text 2 accepts the benefit to senior reviewers and adds a protective benefit for junior participants. A contradicts its opening acknowledgment. B introduces a comparison between scientific disciplines absent from the text. C invents a methodological objection to the sample. The second author broadens the account of beneficiaries rather than rejecting the reported effect or assessing the research design.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Calix Nordan's 1912 novel The Blue Cabinet. Rima is a junior map restorer newly assigned to a survey station; the superintendent manages the station.

To escape the anxious thoughts that had followed her there, Rima began inventing coastlines on a spare slate in the copying room. Whenever the superintendent left on his rounds, she slipped inside and let islands grow beneath the chalk. One afternoon she was explaining an elaborate inlet to the gardener when an unexpectedly early footstep sounded outside. The superintendent noticed the light through the glass door and called to ask who was using the room. Rima had already put the chalk aside and hurried into the passage.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the structure of the text as a whole?

choices.A: A character adopts a diverting activity, and that activity is interrupted on a particular occasion.
choices.B: A character acquires an absorbing new passion, then permanently abandons it after recognizing that it disturbs others.
choices.C: A character first explores her surroundings enthusiastically, then withdraws into growing isolation.
choices.D: A character encounters a crisis, then devises a successful remedy for it.

questions.explanation: A matches the new diversion and the specific interruption caused by the superintendent's early return. B adds permanence, a passion, and recognition of others' discomfort, none of which is established. C mistakes relief from anxiety for enthusiastic exploration and overlooks the gardener's participation. D treats the ending as a solved predicament, although Rima's departure leaves its outcome unknown. The excerpt shows interruption, not a completed resolution.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Harriet Dain's 1910 poem “The Final Key.” The speaker encounters a locksmith beside a city canal.

She drew her sleeve across her face
And turned as if to leave the place;
A small brass key lay in her palm,
Yet nothing in her bearing spoke of calm.
“What loss,” I asked, “has brought you here?”
She held the key and answered through a tear:
“This opened doors I kept for years;
The others went with debts and fears.
Today they closed the last for me;
This is the final workshop key.”
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the poem?

choices.A: The speaker asks a direct question, then expresses regret for having asked it.
choices.B: The speaker finds a new acquaintance, then seeks comfort in being alone.
choices.C: The speaker begins an exchange, then abruptly ends it before receiving an answer.
choices.D: The speaker observes distress, then learns the specific circumstance responsible for it.

questions.explanation: D is correct because the locksmith's gesture and tear first reveal distress, and her answer identifies the closure of her last workshop as its cause. A invents regret on the speaker's part. B adds a turn to solitude rather than an exchange. C contradicts the poem's completed answer. The key initially appears as an unexplained object and then becomes evidence of the loss she describes.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Public benches once offered neighborhoods a visible way to distinguish themselves. Locally made seats varied in carved patterns, wood, and ironwork, making their surroundings recognizable. Current procurement favors repeated concrete forms and a narrow palette of finishes. With those standardized objects, community-specific expression through street furniture is no longer possible.

Text 2
Street furniture still provides opportunities for a neighborhood to express its character. Residents can add mosaics to approved bench panels or surround repeated planters with locally designed tile borders. They can also choose alternatives to the standard forms: several districts have restored older cast-iron seat designs for just this reason. A shared manufactured base need not prevent a distinctive public appearance.
questions.question: Which choice best describes a difference in how the authors portray street furniture?

choices.A: Text 1 predicts declining use of public benches, whereas Text 2 predicts increasing use.
choices.B: Text 1 analyzes benches and planters, whereas Text 2 ignores both kinds of object.
choices.C: Text 1 denies that street furniture can still express local identity, whereas Text 2 maintains that it can.
choices.D: Text 1 lists historically influential designs, whereas Text 2 rejects any association between street furniture and public expression.

questions.explanation: C captures the direct disagreement between the first text's claim of impossibility and the second text's examples of customization and alternative designs. A invents opposing popularity forecasts. B is contradicted by Text 2's explicit benches and planters. D misstates Text 2's central defense of public expression. The dispute concerns expressive possibilities despite standardization, not how many people use the objects.

questions.passage:
The following text is from Maro Selwyn's 1938 novel The South Window.

I had begun to ask Letha whether the final proof should go into the cabinet, but the question lost its shape before I could finish. Her face made every ordinary instruction seem absurd. <u>Her lips had the pale color of primer, the shutter lever clicked against the table in her unsteady hand, and her eyes looked past my shoulder toward the dark square of the workshop window.</u> It seemed that the whole room had spoken a language she alone understood, and that none of its words permitted her to move.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It repeats an uncertainty that the narrator had explicitly voiced in the preceding statements.
choices.B: It supplies details that explain the narrator's interrupted question and reaction.
choices.C: It signals that the descriptions in the following sentence should be considered unreliable.
choices.D: It introduces an exaggeration that the next sentence proceeds to test.

questions.explanation: B is correct because the pallor, unsteady hand, and fixed gaze explain why the narrator cannot continue an ordinary question. A invents an explicitly voiced uncertainty; the earlier statements describe interruption and reaction. C mistakes heightened description for a warning about reliability. D invents a test of an exaggeration; the following metaphor develops the impression of paralysis. The sentence provides the visible basis for the response already narrated.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Ivo Cerane's 1921 poem “Before the New Engine.”

I could not name the hands that made it breathe,
Nor tell what balance taught the brass to sing;
A pulse seemed hidden in each turning ring,
And motion flowered in the gears beneath.
Among the gathered watchers, wordless, still,
I stood before that patient, living will.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the poem?

choices.A: To explain the particular mechanical operation performed by an engine
choices.B: To show the speaker changing from indifference to admiration
choices.C: To justify admiration for an engine that other observers dismiss
choices.D: To convey the powerful impression an engine makes on the speaker

questions.explanation: D fits the animated descriptions of breathing brass, hidden pulse, flowering motion, and the speaker's wordless response. A requires a functional explanation that the poem does not supply; the speaker admits not knowing how the balance works. B invents initial indifference. C invents other observers' dismissal, although they are gathered around the engine. The poem records the force of an encounter rather than explaining mechanics or defending a disputed judgment.

questions.passage:
Text 1
In a 2023 study, ornithologists Alina Verc and Tomas Rell examined how migratory birds selected stopover sites. Seeking fuller evidence on a sparsely measured question, the team compared food availability, vegetation cover, and predator activity across 42 locations. <u>The relative importance of these factors changed with the expected stay: available food best predicted brief stopover choices, while dense cover mattered more during longer stays.</u>

Text 2
Studies of animal behavior may overturn expectations or give solid support to an intuitively plausible account. Verc and Rell's stopover study belongs to the latter group. That birds needing a quick refueling stop favor food, while birds remaining longer need shelter, is not astonishing. The study's breadth and careful comparisons nonetheless turn a reasonable expectation into an empirically grounded finding.
questions.question: How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined statement in Text 1?

choices.A: By treating the conclusions as valuable even though their central pattern is unsurprising
choices.B: By praising the results while questioning the rigor with which the team obtained them
choices.C: By describing ways birds resist the behavior the researchers reported
choices.D: By arguing that a study intended to confirm everyday assumptions necessarily produces startling findings

questions.explanation: A is correct because Text 2 explicitly distinguishes an unsurprising pattern from the value of careful empirical support. B reverses its approval of the study's rigor. C invents counterexamples or resistance that Text 2 never discusses. D contradicts the statement that the findings are not astonishing and adds a rule about research intentions. The author would qualify any suggestion of novelty without dismissing the conclusions' evidentiary importance.

questions.passage:
Text 1
<u>The Vernic canal boom, spanning roughly 1560 to 1780, joined water management with skills more often associated with other trades.</u> Modern accounts tend to emphasize excavation and masonry, yet precision gear-cutting techniques developed by clockmakers helped shape the sluice machinery at Halden Locks in 1772. The project demonstrates how canal builders drew on an unexpectedly different technical tradition.

Text 2
Calling Vernic canal engineering “clockwork-like” is most appropriate to the later part of the boom. From the 1680s onward, closely fitted gear trains regulated increasingly elaborate gates; the machinery at Halden Locks is a notable example. Earlier works, especially those built before 1650, depended chiefly on levers, wedges, and laborers' direct handling of gates. Precision gearing was thus characteristic of a phase, not uniformly of the whole period.
questions.question: How would the author of Text 2 most likely regard the underlined characterization in Text 1?

choices.A: As a misunderstanding of the distinctive machinery installed at Halden Locks
choices.B: As an unsuccessful attempt to extend clockmaking's influence beyond excavation and masonry
choices.C: As an apt illustration of a trend associated with a particular phase of the canal boom
choices.D: As an error about how clockmaking techniques shaped the earliest Vernic canals

questions.explanation: C follows Text 2's acceptance of Halden Locks as an example of later precision gearing. The author would contextualize the example in a particular phase. A invents disagreement about the machinery itself. B misstates the relationship among the trades and ignores Text 2's endorsement of the example. D locates the 1772 project in the earliest phase, contrary to the chronology. Qualifying a broad period label does not require rejecting a valid later example.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Nerra Talon's 1947 novel Margins of Air.

<u>For the next three flying seasons, Ceryn watched the ground below with an attention that needed no prompting.</u> Roads, field boundaries, the changes in color beside a stream: all entered her mind before she thought to select among them. Her memory was less a notebook she kept than a drawer that filled itself whenever the aircraft banked. Years later, when she had to judge an unfamiliar landing ground at a glance, she would draw on that unplanned accumulation with a precision that surprised those who had mistaken her quiet watching for idleness.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It identifies the remembered observations that eventually proved most important to Ceryn.
choices.B: It characterizes Ceryn's habitual mental activity during a particular period.
choices.C: It explains the cause of Ceryn's fascination with other people aboard the aircraft.
choices.D: It depicts Ceryn as excessively absorbed in examining her own emotions.

questions.explanation: B is correct because the sentence specifies a period and Ceryn's spontaneous attentiveness during it. Later sentences elaborate how those impressions accumulate and become useful. A mistakes the broad habit for a selection of particular memories. C supplies a cause and a focus on other passengers that the sentence does not contain. D shifts attention from the external landscape to Ceryn's emotions. The sentence establishes the mental pattern developed throughout the excerpt.

questions.passage: Historian Esmé Tralen investigates overlooked domestic labor by combining household accounts, interviews, and spatial records in different proportions. For her 2014 Harbor Hours project, she spent a month following the paths through which meals and laundry reached seasonal dockworkers, documenting tasks absent from payrolls. A later project, The Uncounted Day, approached similar questions through a different arrangement of evidence. Published in 2021, it placed family time-use notebooks beside official employment registers, with blank columns marking work the registers never recorded. The juxtaposition encouraged readers to reconsider what an apparently complete employment history leaves invisible.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It praises one researcher, then introduces a second whose work has become more influential.
choices.B: It describes one project, then identifies the experiences that inspired it.
choices.C: It begins favorably, then turns to criticism of the same researcher's later work.
choices.D: It states a general account of a researcher's approach, then illustrates that account with particular projects.

questions.explanation: D matches the opening statement about Tralen's combined methods and the two projects showing different uses of those methods. A invents a second researcher. B reduces two examples to one project and substitutes origins for descriptions. C mistakes a change in evidence for a change to unfavorable assessment. The text develops its initial characterization through examples rather than redirecting its judgment.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Mira Deren's 2019 novel The Unfinished House confronts the practical and emotional aftermath of a coastal flood, but it includes one fantastic device: certain walls repair themselves overnight. These “renewing rooms” are both unsettling and hopeful. They connect the family's struggles through a series of unexpected transformations, allowing Deren to juxtapose material restoration with a humane account of relationships that cannot be repaired so automatically.

Text 2
The “renewing rooms” weaken rather than enrich The Unfinished House. A novel about recovering from a flood ought to confront the cost, delay, and possible failure involved in rebuilding. By restoring walls overnight, Deren sidesteps those constraints in an otherwise grounded narrative. The family's emotions remain, but the practical ordeal central to the novel's circumstances becomes less fully represented.
questions.question: Which choice best describes a difference between the authors' assessments of the “renewing rooms”?

choices.A: Text 2 is substantially less favorable toward the device than Text 1 is.
choices.B: Text 2 finds the device more difficult to explain than Text 1 does.
choices.C: Text 1 treats the device as peripheral, whereas Text 2 considers it central.
choices.D: Text 1 regards the device as realistic, whereas Text 2 regards it as imaginary.

questions.explanation: A is correct because Text 1 praises the device's imaginative and humane possibilities, whereas Text 2 argues that it removes important constraints from the subject. B invents difficulty explaining the device. C understates its integral role in Text 1's account. D ignores Text 1's explicit identification of it as fantastic. Both recognize the device's nature and importance; they differ over whether it strengthens the novel's treatment of its topic.

questions.passage: Marine chemist Narek Yilan's concern with the boundary between fresh and salt water culminated in the 1976 monograph The Salt Boundary, a work valued for its synthesis of estuarine processes. That synthesis followed several attempts Yilan never published. Earlier in the decade, he prepared an extended set of notes on how small changes in salinity could reshape plankton communities, then destroyed the draft rather than circulate it. A lecture sequence on the same problem likewise remained unpublished and has not survived. These abandoned accounts suggest that the subject occupied him well before it reached its definitive published form.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?

choices.A: To suggest that Yilan found his publications after The Salt Boundary unsatisfactory
choices.B: To contrast The Salt Boundary with earlier projects mainly in terms of their ambition
choices.C: To identify connections between The Salt Boundary and several earlier unpublished efforts
choices.D: To trace changes in Yilan's methods during the actual composition of The Salt Boundary

questions.explanation: C is correct because the monograph and abandoned notes and lectures share Yilan's concern with fresh-salt boundaries and related plankton changes. A refers to later publications not discussed. B makes comparative ambition central, although the text emphasizes a sustained subject. D confines the chronology to composition of the final monograph and invents methodological change. The earlier efforts explain the depth of the preoccupation, rather than establish a before-and-after method.

questions.passage: In 2011, surveyors in Argentina's Valle de Lura found that groundwater at widely separated wells was becoming saline. Geochemical tests traced the change to an unusually extensive underground brine reservoir, a feature whose size attracted attention beyond the original water survey. Researchers subsequently began mapping isotope signatures in samples from the reservoir and surrounding aquifers. <u>Such a map could explain how brine reaches distant wells and identify places where barriers might reduce further mixing with usable groundwater.</u>
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It shows that the original surveyors have personally continued every phase of the investigation.
choices.B: It describes potential explanatory and practical implications of the isotope-mapping research.
choices.C: It demonstrates how many new questions have already been answered about the reservoir.
choices.D: It offers a conclusion that contradicts the earlier explanation for salinity in the wells.

questions.explanation: B is correct because the sentence identifies two possible benefits: explaining the brine's spread and locating opportunities to limit mixing. A invents continuity of personnel. C changes potential outcomes into completed answers and claims a quantity of results the text does not give. D falsely creates a contradiction; tracing the reservoir's routes develops the earlier explanation. The conditional 'could' marks implications rather than achieved findings.

questions.passage: A colored stripe through a crowded terminal is more than decoration. Such markings, variously called “floor trails” and “wayfinding bands,” have been assigned different roles over the past seventy years. Some designers see them chiefly as reassurance: a visible route reduces uncertainty in an unfamiliar building. For industrial organizer Olya Sar, however, the same idea served efficiency. Her company, Strand Systems, introduced patterned routes in 1946, and she promoted them as a way to coordinate movements between work areas. A sequence of colored junctions could, she claimed, keep separate crews from interrupting one another's tasks.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the purpose of the text?

choices.A: To defend one use of floor markings after cataloging several alternatives
choices.B: To investigate Sar's personality through controversies surrounding her company
choices.C: To describe floor markings and identify roles that different people attribute to them
choices.D: To recount the origin of floor markings and refute objections to them

questions.explanation: C captures the description and the two attributed functions: reassurance and coordinated efficiency. A incorrectly gives the author a final advocacy position; Sar's claim is reported rather than endorsed as the sole proper use. B invents a personality analysis and controversies. D adds criticism and rebuttal not present in the text. The historical detail supports the account of one attributed role without making the whole passage an origin story.

questions.passage:
Text 1
A single thin bamboo ribbon cannot support a substantial shelf, but woven assemblies of such ribbons point toward surprisingly strong structures. Researchers at Pelvar Materials Lab have built small demonstration racks whose interlocking strips distribute loads across many points. The individual components remain light and flexible; joined in sufficient numbers, they hold objects far heavier than one ribbon could carry.

Text 2
The promise of thin structural strips lies largely in assemblies rather than isolated components. Layered or woven groups can fulfill building tasks while remaining more adaptable than one rigid beam. They can also distribute the consequences of damage: when one strip breaks, surrounding strips continue carrying part of its load. Strength and resilience therefore need not depend on making every component large.
questions.question: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Combining many small components can enable a load-bearing task that one component could not accomplish alone.
choices.B: Current ribbon designs were originally intended as miniature versions of large rigid beams.
choices.C: Using renewable bamboo directly eliminates every source of fragility in a large structure.
choices.D: Tasks performed by ribbon assemblies are currently completed most efficiently through continuous manual supervision.

questions.explanation: A is supported by Text 1's heavier loads and Text 2's building tasks completed by assemblies. B invents the original design intention. C assigns resilience directly to renewability and makes an absolute claim; Text 2 attributes it to distributing loads across components. D introduces an efficiency comparison and supervision requirement absent from both texts. Their shared point concerns collective capacity, even though each text emphasizes a different advantage.

questions.passage:
The following text is from Orel Merin's 1908 novel The Third Workshop.

Few apprentices lingered after work, and fewer still returned for an unrequired lesson. Director Savel had made even capable visitors dislike his company; their accomplishments served him chiefly as occasions to explain how far they remained beneath his own. They could obtain instruction elsewhere without paying for it in humiliation. <u>His partner, Edda, achieved much the same solitude by inspiring apprehension rather than resentment.</u> Exacting and impatient, she could turn an innocent question into an examination whose outcome no visitor wished to risk.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It conveys the repellent physical features of the workshop setting.
choices.B: It explains the origins of Savel's habit of regarding visitors as inferior.
choices.C: It introduces another character whose effect on visitors is comparable to Savel's.
choices.D: It contrasts Savel's character with the traits of visitors who dislike him.

questions.explanation: C is correct because Edda, like Savel, discourages company, though her visitors feel apprehension rather than resentment. The sentence establishes a parallel outcome and introduces her subsequent characterization. A shifts from people to physical surroundings. B invents an account of how Savel developed his attitude. D misidentifies Edda as one of the visitors instead of his partner. The difference in emotional response does not erase the comparison in social effect.

questions.passage:
The following text is from Malika Dorn's 1928 novel The Borrowed Compass.

Azra and I shared lodgings at the survey academy, and much of what I learned there came from conversations outside our classes. <u>For all her delight in practical jokes, she was a careful student, with an absorbing private interest in acoustics.</u> She would explain why a tuning fork answered differently beside a hollow tube, or why a low note lingered in one room and vanished in another. By the end of that winter, I recognized problems of resonance and reflection that our formal exercises had scarcely touched.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It develops a previously described disagreement between Azra and the narrator.
choices.B: It identifies characteristics of Azra that the following account further illustrates.
choices.C: It suggests a source of interpersonal tension subsequently revealed in the excerpt.
choices.D: It gives more information about the formal curriculum outlined in the preceding sentence.

questions.explanation: B is correct because Azra's seriousness and interest in acoustics are illustrated by the explanations she gives and the knowledge the narrator gains. A and C invent conflict; the relationship is presented as intellectually useful. D mistakes learning outside classes for an outline of the formal curriculum. The qualification about jokes contrasts aspects of Azra herself, not her relationship with the narrator.

questions.passage: Turning a detailed technical handbook into a software interface can raise fears that the original author's judgment will be lost. That concern is misplaced in the case of Alina Ferex's 2011 Relland Handbook, which became an inspection interface in 2018. Ferex co-led the interface's design, making her own treatment of uncertain measurements part of its operation. The handbook's careful distinction between a questionable reading and a confirmed defect consequently survived in the controls and prompts users encountered. The change of format did not require abandoning the distinctions central to Ferex's work.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To argue that the interface retained the central judgments of Ferex's original handbook
choices.B: To speculate about what motivated Ferex to write the original handbook
choices.C: To describe the style and full content of the Relland Handbook
choices.D: To demonstrate that most conversions of technical writing into software are fundamentally flawed

questions.explanation: A follows the stated concern, the account of Ferex's involvement, and the example of a distinction preserved in the interface. B asks about a motive the text does not explore. C reduces the passage to a content description, overlooking its argument about faithful conversion. D generalizes a problem to most conversions despite the successful case the passage presents. The handbook detail functions as evidence of retained judgment.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Mara Sefar's 1919 short story “Sounding Duty.” The narrator is an apprentice surveyor.

Captain Halver examined the fresh chart sheets one by one, his satisfaction becoming more visible with each page. “These will make them listen to us,” he said. “You must not soften the dangerous reaches.”

Later he summoned me to his cabin, and I went with a fear I could neither account for nor dismiss.

“You will take charge of the next sounding,” he said. “You came from Fen District; surely you know its channels and its people better than anyone here.”

<u>“I believe I do,” I answered, while my fingers shook against the chart case.</u>
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion?

choices.A: It illustrates the narrator's usual response to Halver's routine inspection of charts.
choices.B: It explains why the task Halver assigns will be technically difficult to complete.
choices.C: It reveals the narrator's eager wish to please Halver through a difficult assignment.
choices.D: It makes the narrator's emotional state evident in the response to Halver's directions.

questions.explanation: D is correct because the spoken assent is accompanied by shaking fingers, making the narrator's fear visible in the response to the assignment. A ignores the specific directive and the unusual fear described before it. B supplies a technical reason for difficulty that the sentence does not contain. C mistakes anxious compliance for demonstrated eagerness to please. The words and physical detail reveal emotion without establishing its full cause.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Conservation brushes have become remarkably specialized for reaching surfaces that ordinary painting brushes cannot treat. In the Ravelin restoration archive, worn tools show narrow tips developed for deep grooves and flattened bundles suited to broad but fragile finishes. Researchers studying the archive relate those variations to the increasing range of surfaces conservators needed to handle.

Text 2
In her 2016 article “The Shapes of Conservation,” tool historian Elira Sen notes that the variety of conservation brushes includes more than 430 documented designs. Despite this diversity, many share a division within the bristle bundle: outer fibers carry liquid to the surface, while a stiffer inner core maintains the bundle's shape. Sen finds the many specialized forms more striking than any one shared structural feature.
questions.question: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Their bristle arrangement supports both liquid delivery and retention of the bundle's shape.
choices.B: Different designs emerged as conservators adapted their tools to particular kinds of surface.
choices.C: Conservation brushes are noteworthy for the extent of their specialization.
choices.D: Many conservation brushes share an internal division despite differences in their external forms.

questions.explanation: C is supported by Text 1's surface-specific forms and Text 2's explicit emphasis on many specialized designs. A and D describe the bristle organization discussed only in Text 2; Text 1 supplies no account of internal structure. B captures the surface-based explanation offered only in Text 1; Text 2 does not explain how those designs arose. The question requires support in both accounts, rather than a statement established in just one.

questions.passage: <u>A central disagreement among reservoir engineers after the 1960s concerned Arven Dale's “single-outlet” model and Nara Bels's “distributed-flow” model.</u> For Dale, one principal outlet largely determined the drainage behavior of an entire reservoir system; changes at that outlet could transform conditions elsewhere. Bels instead emphasized a network of smaller passages. Within her model, several alternative routes could perform similar functions, so assigning a uniquely decisive role to one outlet overlooked the system's capacity to redistribute flow.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It explains how interchangeability is central to Bels's model but not to Dale's.
choices.B: It surveys the specific events that caused the two models to be proposed.
choices.C: It introduces models that both make one exceptional outlet decisive.
choices.D: It presents opposing accounts that the subsequent sentences explain more fully.

questions.explanation: D is correct because the opening identifies a disagreement and names its two models, which the following sentences unpack. A describes one important contrast developed later, not the information supplied in the underlined sentence. B invents an account of formative events. C contradicts the opposition: only Dale assigns a uniquely decisive role to one outlet. The opening frames the comparison without itself detailing either mechanism.

questions.passage: Early signal stations on the Gareth Vale railway used colored arms and lanterns to communicate with approaching crews. <u>An operator raised an arm against a pale backing board by day, while a lantern displayed a colored shape through the same opening after dark.</u> Plain though that arrangement appears, the stations conveyed a considerable range of instructions. Arm contours made positions distinguishable at a distance, and additional devices, including patterned flashes, shaded panes, and short bell sequences, helped separate an urgent stop from a caution or permission to proceed slowly.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It identifies an innovation that first made complex instructions compatible with simple equipment.
choices.B: It visually describes an arrangement whose communicative range the text subsequently analyzes.
choices.C: It lists the physical traits responsible for the popularity of a railway's signals.
choices.D: It explains why the traditional signal arrangement resisted later modification.

questions.explanation: B is correct because the sentence describes what approaching crews would see, before later sentences discuss how that apparently plain arrangement supports varied instructions. A makes a historical claim about a first innovation and a causal explanation that the sentence does not provide. C adds popularity and confuses the initial visual setup with the later account of distinguishing features. D invents resistance to change. Description prepares for analysis of versatility rather than itself establishing its causes.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Can perceived delivery reliability be measured? Assigning numbers to customers' confidence seems difficult, but some rating methods have proved useful. The Delivery Predictability Scale has allowed researchers to compare confidence among small groups of recipients. Such self-reports may be less dependable if extended from a limited study to an entire urban distribution network.

Text 2
Analyst Kira Rann's research suggests that valued predictability can be estimated in monetary terms. Avoiding reliance on confidence ratings alone, her team combined observed purchasing decisions with a statistical model. Customers were willing to pay an additional $5.80 for a delivery window narrowed from two hours to ninety minutes, according to Rann's 2021 article “The Price of a Time Window.” The finding supplies a quantitative estimate of how much a reduction in uncertainty mattered to those customers.
questions.question: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Researchers have achieved some success in quantifying aspects of valued delivery predictability.
choices.B: Monetary models are consistently superior to rating scales for evaluating delivery services.
choices.C: Rann's model fails to account adequately for the subjective responses of customers.
choices.D: Statistical models can determine all benefits of predictable deliveries for an entire society.

questions.explanation: A is the modest common ground: Text 1 identifies useful ratings in small studies, and Text 2 reports a monetary estimate from observed choices. B requires a general ranking that neither author establishes. C attributes a failure to Rann that neither text identifies. D expands a limited customer finding into all societal benefits. The first author's concern about scale does not negate the acknowledged success of bounded quantitative research.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Visitors to the Taren Sound Archive encounter several regional forms of speech, including the Rellin language. One listening station lets visitors hear a short exchange and then record their own attempt at a phrase. Alongside films and annotated transcripts, such activities encourage care for the linguistic traditions preserved in the collection.

Text 2
Rellin's long decline in everyday use has recently stabilized. Raising awareness of the language is worthwhile, but its continued use owes more to coordinated teaching than to public displays alone. The partnership behind a 2022 revitalization program brought family groups, local schools, and language educators together to create regular opportunities to speak Rellin. Those efforts provided continuity that occasional encounters at an archive could not ensure by themselves.
questions.question: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Every regional language represented in the archive has begun to flourish.
choices.B: Educational activities such as those offered by the Taren Sound Archive have value.
choices.C: Rellin can be presented in an archive only because its number of speakers has increased substantially.
choices.D: Educating more archive visitors would necessarily produce additional teaching partnerships.

questions.explanation: B is supported by Text 1's favorable account of engagement and Text 2's explicit acknowledgment that awareness is worthwhile. A generalizes one language's stabilization to every regional language. C invents both a substantial increase and a condition for archival presentation. D assigns a guaranteed causal effect to education that neither passage establishes. The second author can value awareness while assigning greater responsibility for continued use to coordinated teaching.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Nerise Avon's 1895 poem “Beyond the Lanterns.” The “you” addressed by the speaker is a bell buoy in the harbor.

You lift upon the swell,
A red rim briefly showing;
Above the water's dull farewell
Your little fire is glowing,
Then sinks where darker currents dwell.
The low white mist draws near
And folds your painted turning;
No edge remains to make you clear,
No color keeps its burning,
But still your measured bell I hear.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the poem?

choices.A: The speaker addresses the buoy, then turns to address the poem's reader.
choices.B: The speaker compares the buoy with the harbor, then contrasts its movement with human customs.
choices.C: The speaker admires the buoy, then reveals growing intimidation.
choices.D: The speaker describes the buoy's visible movement, then notes its sound when it is obscured.

questions.explanation: D follows the progression from lifting, shining, and sinking to mist hiding the buoy while its bell remains audible. A invents a change in addressee. B adds a comparison with human customs that never appears. C interprets darkening and mist as the speaker's intimidation without evidence. The change concerns the mode of perception, from seeing movement and color to hearing the continuing bell.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Computer researchers have observed growing instability in the Athen municipal archives as incoming files become larger and more numerous. Technology reporter Sena Lark notes that “incoming data volume is growing at twice the rate anticipated in the original capacity plan.” High-resolution images now make up more of each upload than short text files do, placing heavier demands on storage operations and increasing brief service failures.

Text 2
Researcher Pek Orne told the Haven Technical Review that “we now see bursts of failed writes after unusually large uploads.” He also describes a change in scheduling: processes once initiated in planned batches are increasingly “upload-led,” starting as soon as live submissions arrive. Similar pressures in archives outside Athen suggest that rising input loads are linked to the disruption rather than being a purely local peculiarity.
questions.question: How would the researchers cited in Text 1 most likely respond to Orne's remarks about unusually large uploads in Text 2?

choices.A: By agreeing that increased incoming data loads are causing difficulties in the archives
choices.B: By asserting that some consequences of larger uploads have chiefly been beneficial
choices.C: By criticizing Orne for ignoring all changes in how archive processes are scheduled
choices.D: By insisting that storage failures pose a greater threat than the uploads that precede them

questions.explanation: A is supported by both accounts linking larger incoming loads with disruption. B introduces benefits that Text 1 does not describe. C contradicts Text 2's discussion of changing schedules. D imposes a ranking between a problem and its proposed cause that neither account makes. The authors' shared concern is the effect of increased input, even though Text 2 adds a scheduling change and broader comparisons.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Teren Alda's 1956 drama The Unnumbered Bench. An “Associate” is a laboratory worker on a limited temporary contract; the “Director” heads the institute.

FIRST ASSOCIATE: Fourteen months I have spent preparing those crystal plates, and each usable reading cost me an evening when the others had gone home. This new series I reserved for my own study of heat passing through the coatings. Then our Director came down to the bench, examined the numbered trays, and instructed the clerk to enter the entire series beneath his name. He remained there until the last page had been filed. If even the observations we make disappear into another person's name, by what work are associates to establish a place for themselves?
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To evoke the speaker's peaceful contentment with laboratory work
choices.B: To establish that the Director's behavior is unusual for people in his position
choices.C: To communicate the speaker's sense of having been treated unjustly
choices.D: To explain the speaker's customary duties within the institute

questions.explanation: C is correct because the speaker contrasts prolonged personal effort and an intended study with the Director's appropriation of credit, then questions how associates can advance under such conditions. A contradicts the complaint. B requires a comparison with typical directors that the speech does not provide. D makes background duties the central purpose, overlooking the grievance and rhetorical question. The details of work establish the basis of the perceived injustice.
